opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a really interesting question, and I think people sometimes underestimate how subtle it is.

The basic intuition behind consensus is sound. If you sample from several models, or sample the same model many times, and they converge on the same answer, that's usually a signal of higher confidence. We've seen this for a long time with things like self-consistency and majority voting on math problems. It works because when a model is wrong, it tends to be wrong in different ways, while when it's right, the answers cluster.

But that assumption breaks down in a few important places. The first is correlated errors. If the models you're routing between were trained on similar data with similar techniques, they can all confidently agree on the wrong answer. Consensus then gives you false confidence, which is arguably worse than no signal at all. So when I evaluate one of these systems, the first thing I want to know is how independent the models actually are, and whether the routing layer is calibrated: when it says "high agreement," is it actually right more often?

The second issue is that consensus favors the median answer. That's great for questions with a clear verifiable answer, but on hard problems the best answer is often the one that only the strongest model, or the model that thought the longest, finds. A majority vote can drown out the one reasoning chain that actually got it. This is a big part of why I'm excited about reasoning models and test-time compute: often a single model thinking longer beats aggregating a bunch of quick answers. So you have to compare against that baseline, not just against a single cheap sample.

Third, you need to measure the whole tradeoff, not only accuracy. Consensus costs compute and latency. A good routing layer should be adaptive: if the question is easy and the cheap models agree, stop there. If they disagree, escalate to a stronger model or spend more thinking time. That's a lot like how we approached search in poker and Diplomacy. You spend compute where the uncertainty is.

So concretely, I'd evaluate on a few axes: accuracy on held-out tasks, especially hard ones where the frontier model alone is the right comparison; calibration of the agreement signal; performance on adversarial or out-of-distribution cases where correlated failures show up; and cost and latency at a fixed accuracy target. And I'd be careful about benchmarks with clean verifiable answers, because consensus looks best there. The real test is messier, open-ended tasks where "agreement" is harder even to define.

r001.rationale: The response recommends measuring cost and latency at a fixed accuracy target, but does not propose plotting benchmark performance against token usage or cost on the x-axis.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, because consensus is one of those ideas that sounds obviously good and turns out to be really subtle when you try to measure it.

The first thing I'd say is that you have to separate two questions. One is: does the routing layer pick the right model for a given query? And the other is: does aggregating multiple models actually produce a better answer than the best single model would have? People conflate these constantly. You can have a router that's great at the first and the consensus mechanism adds nothing, or vice versa.

For the consensus piece specifically, the thing I always want to know is how correlated the errors are. If you have five models that were all trained on roughly the same internet data with roughly the same post-training recipes, they're going to be confidently wrong in the same places. Majority vote doesn't help you there. It just gives you a false sense of security, because now you have agreement, and agreement feels like evidence. So when I evaluate these systems, I want to look specifically at the cases where the ensemble is unanimous and wrong. That's the failure mode that matters, because it's the one where the system can't even flag its own uncertainty.

The second thing is that the benefit of consensus is really domain-dependent, and it tracks closely with how verifiable the task is. In something like math or code, where you can check the answer, you don't really need consensus. You need a verifier. Sample a bunch of times, run the tests, pick the one that passes. That's a much stronger signal than models agreeing with each other. Where consensus becomes interesting is in the fuzzy domains, where there's no ground truth to check against. But those are also exactly the domains where it's hardest to evaluate whether consensus helped, because your eval is itself going to be some kind of judgment call.

And then there's the cost dimension, which people underweight. If you're calling five models to answer a question, you've spent five times the compute. The honest comparison isn't consensus versus a single call to one model. It's consensus versus spending that same compute budget on a single strong model thinking longer, or sampling more and verifying. In my experience that comparison is often not flattering to the consensus approach. Test-time compute scaling within one model tends to be more sample-efficient than averaging across models, because the model can actually build on its own reasoning rather than just voting.

So if I were building the eval, I'd want: a breakdown by domain, a specific look at correlated failures, and a compute-matched baseline. If a routing layer can beat a single frontier model at equal cost on tasks that matter, that's a real result. If it only wins when you let it spend more, I'm much less impressed.

r001.rationale: The response recommends a compute-matched baseline, but does not propose plotting benchmark performance against token usage or cost on the x-axis.

astra-6.text:
I’d separate agreement from correctness. If you ask five models and they all give the same answer, that might be useful evidence. But if they’re making correlated mistakes, you can get a very confident consensus that’s wrong.

So I’d evaluate the whole system on tasks where you can independently check the answer, and compare it against simpler baselines at the same inference budget. Could you get the same improvement by just using the strongest model, or by giving one model more time to reason? The routing layer needs to beat those alternatives, not just beat a single cheap call.

And I’d look particularly closely at the cases where consensus fails. Does the system recognize uncertainty, or does agreement make it more confident precisely when it shouldn’t be? Ultimately, consensus is a signal you can use in the routing decision. It isn’t itself the evaluation.

r001.rationale: The response recommends comparing performance against alternatives at the same inference budget, but does not propose plotting benchmark performance against token usage or cost on the x-axis.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is whether the models are making independent mistakes. If you ask five models and they all agree, that sounds reassuring, but if they’re all wrong for the same reason, you haven’t gained much.

So I’d evaluate the routing system end to end on problems where you can actually check the answer. Does agreement predict correctness? When the models disagree, does the router know which one to trust, or when to spend more compute? And then compare that against a simple baseline: using the strongest individual model at the same overall cost.

Consensus can be a useful signal. But I wouldn’t treat consensus itself as the measure of success. The measure is whether you get more reliable answers for the resources you spend.

r001.rationale: The response suggests comparing reliability at the same overall cost, but does not propose plotting benchmark performance against token usage or cost on the x-axis.
